meta.title: Who really said "Management is efficiency in climbing the ladder of success; leadership determines whether the ladder is leaning against the right wall"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Covey’s own line: The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People (1989), p. 101. The sentence before it isn’t his, and the metaphor predates him.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Management is efficiency in climbing the ladder of success; leadership determines whether the ladder is leaning against the right wall'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: page 101 of The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People (1989). The ladder metaphor itself, though, was newspaper filler back in 1915.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This one is real, and unusually well pinned down. It is Covey’s own sentence in The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People: Restoring the Character Ethic, in the chapter on Habit 2, “Begin With the End In Mind” — Quote Investigator prints the whole paragraph and cites it to page 101 of the 1989 Simon and Schuster edition, “verified with scans” ↗, and Wikiquote’s sourced section gives the same book, year and page ↗. Two things are worth knowing anyway: the sentence immediately before it in that paragraph is not his, and the ladder-against-the-wrong-wall image turns up as newspaper filler in 1915, seventeen years before he was born.

source.heading: Page 101, and the paragraph it sits in

source.excerpt: Management is a bottom line focus: How can I best accomplish certain things? Leadership deals with the top line: What are the things I want to accomplish? In the words of both Peter Drucker and Warren Bennis, “Management is doing things right; leadership is doing the right things.” Management is efficiency in climbing the ladder of success; leadership determines whether the ladder is leaning against the right wall.
trail: The anchor is Quote Investigator’s study of the management-versus-leadership sayings. Its 1989 section ↗ reproduces the full Covey paragraph, ladder sentence and all, and gives the citation as “1989, The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People: Restoring the Character Ethic by Stephen R. Covey, Habit 2: Begin With the End In Mind, Quote Page 101, Simon & Schuster, New York. (Verified with scans)”.

Wikiquote agrees independently. The entry ↗ lists the sentence verbatim in a sourced section headed The Seven Habits Of Highly Effective People (1989), cited to p. 101 — not under the page’s Disputed or Misattributed headings.

The book’s own details check out: Wikipedia ↗ gives first publication in 1989 and names Habit 2 as “Begin with the End in Mind,” and the Internet Archive’s catalogue record ↗ holds a borrowable scan of the same text, described as New York: Fireside Book, 1990.

We then checked what Covey is not responsible for. QI’s ladder chronology ↗ shows the wrong-wall image circulating in newspapers from 30 December 1915, tentatively credited to Allen Raine, long before Covey reformulated it; and FranklinCovey’s own Habit 2 page ↗ prints a different Covey ladder sentence rather than this one, which is a fair measure of how easily the variants substitute for each other.
source.excerptNote: Two famous sentences, two different owners. The one Covey wraps in quotation marks he credits to Drucker and Bennis; only the ladder sentence that follows is his. One bibliographic caution, offered for transparency: QI’s separate ladder article ↗ cites a different Covey sentence about the same image at quote page 98 of a printing it dates 1988, while the paragraph above is cited to the 1989 Simon and Schuster edition at page 101. That is an edition difference between two citations for two different sentences, not a conflict about what he wrote.

author.name: Stephen Covey
author.heading: The man who put the ladder against a wall
author.bio: Stephen Richards Covey was born in Salt Lake City in 1932 and died in Idaho Falls in 2012. He took an MBA at Harvard Business School and a doctorate in religious education at Brigham Young University, where he later taught in the Marriott School of Management before holding the Huntsman Presidential Chair at Utah State University’s Jon M. Huntsman School of Business. The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People, first published in 1989, made him one of the most-quoted business writers alive — which is precisely why so many lines he never wrote now carry his name.

copyAttribution: Stephen R. Covey, The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People: Restoring the Character Ethic (New York: Simon & Schuster, 1989), p. 101 — the citation verified against scans by Quote Investigator. Note that the sentence Covey places just before it, "Management is doing things right; leadership is doing the right things," is one he puts in quotation marks and credits to Peter Drucker and Warren Bennis. The older image of a ladder leaning against the wrong wall is traced by Quote Investigator to a Brooklyn Daily Eagle filler item of 30 December 1915.

misattribution.heading: What gets mixed up with it
misattribution.intro: The sentence itself is sound. The confusion is all around it — a neighbour sentence that belongs to other men, an image older than Covey, and a smoothed paraphrase that has quietly replaced his actual wording online.

items.why: In the same paragraph Covey writes, in quotation marks, “In the words of both Peter Drucker and Warren Bennis, ‘Management is doing things right; leadership is doing the right things.’” That one he is explicitly not claiming. Because the two sentences are almost always quoted as a single block, credit slides in both directions — Covey gets the Drucker and Bennis line, and Drucker or Bennis get the ladder. Quote Investigator separates the two ↗.

items.who: Allen Raine — and, before that, an anonymous newspaper column
items.why: Covey coined this sentence, but not the picture in it. Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ finds the thought as a filler item in The Brooklyn Daily Eagle of 30 December 1915 — “You may get to the very top of the ladder, and then find it has not been leaning against the right wall” — attributed there to Allen Raine, a credit QI itself offers only tentatively. The same article logs later credits to a “Mae Maloo,” to H. Jackson Brown Jr. and to Thomas Merton.

items.scope: The wording usually circulated as his
items.why: “You may climb the ladder of success only to find it is leaning against the wrong wall” is pinned on Covey constantly, but it matches neither the page-101 sentence above nor his other ladder sentence. QI records a 1986 Los Angeles Times report ↗ of Covey telling executives they may climb the ladder of success only to find it’s leaning against the wrong wall — a reporter’s rendering of a talk, not his printed prose. His own company prints a third version ↗: “It is incredibly easy to work harder and harder at climbing the ladder of success only to realize that it’s leaning against the wrong wall.”

misattribution.truthLine: So: the sentence on this page is genuinely Covey’s, and it has a page number — page 101 of the 1989 Seven Habits, verified against scans ↗. Just quote it as written there, and leave the Drucker and Bennis line outside the quotation marks around his name.

context.heading: Why the sentence stuck
lead: Covey wrote it as the punchline to a parable. A crew hacks a path through the jungle with machetes; the managers behind them sharpen the machetes, write policy manuals and run productivity programmes; and then somebody climbs the tallest tree, looks around and shouts “Wrong jungle!” The ladder sentence is the same joke made portable — a whole management philosophy compressed into one image you can hold in your head.

That portability is also why it drifted. Covey set his sentence directly after a line he attributed to Peter Drucker and Warren Bennis, so the pair travel together as a block and credit slides between the two names. And the underlying picture — the ladder reaching the top of the wrong wall — was already an old newspaper aphorism when Covey picked it up, which is how a genuinely sourced 1989 sentence ended up entangled with an anonymous scrap from 1915.
context.pull: Only one of the two famous sentences in that paragraph is actually Covey’s. This is the one.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator reproduces Covey's full paragraph including "Management is efficiency in climbing the ladder of success; leadership determines whether the ladder is leaning against the right wall" and cites it to 1989, The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People: Restoring the Character Ethic, Habit 2: Begin With the End In Mind, Quote Page 101, Simon & Schuster, New York, marked "(Verified with scans)". The same article credits Drucker with the efficiency/effectiveness versions (1963 Harvard Business Review, 1965 Financial Post, 1974 Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices) and Bennis with the leadership/management variant.

Wikiquote's Stephen Covey page lists the exact sentence in its sourced section headed "The Seven Habits Of Highly Effective People (1989)", cited to p. 101 (not under Disputed or Misattributed). The page also gives Covey's dates as October 24, 1932 - July 16, 2012.

Quote Investigator traces the ladder-against-the-wrong-wall saying to a Brooklyn Daily Eagle item of 30 December 1915 - "You may get to the very top of the ladder, and then find it has not been leaning against the right wall" - attributed to Allen Raine, whom it tentatively credits as originator; logs a 1986 Los Angeles Times report of Covey telling business executives "they may climb the ladder of success only to find it's leaning against the wrong wall"; cites Covey's different sentence "work harder and harder at climbing the ladder of success only to discover it's leaning against the wrong wall" at page 98 of a printing it dates 1988; and records later credits to Mae Maloo (1972), H. Jackson Brown Jr. (1990) and Thomas Merton (2011).
Wikipedia gives The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People as first published in 1989, publisher Free Press, author Stephen R. Covey, and describes Habit 2 as "Begin with the End in Mind".

Wikipedia gives Stephen Richards Covey as born 24 October 1932 in Salt Lake City and died 16 July 2012 in Idaho Falls; MBA from Harvard Business School; doctorate in religious education from Brigham Young University; professor at BYU's Marriott School of Management; later held the Huntsman Presidential Chair at Utah State University's Jon M. Huntsman School of Business.

FranklinCovey's own Habit 2 page quotes Covey as "It is incredibly easy to work harder and harder at climbing the ladder of success only to realize that it's leaning against the wrong wall" and does NOT contain the "Management is efficiency in climbing the ladder of success" sentence.

The Internet Archive holds a borrowable scan of the book catalogued as "The seven habits of highly effective people : restoring the character ethic", creator Covey, Stephen R., date 1990, publisher New York : Fireside Book (confirmed via the archive.org metadata endpoint for identifier sevenhabitsofhig0000cove_y9t8).

Negative check - ManageMagazine's collection of Peter Drucker quotes does not attribute any "ladder of success" or "leaning against the right wall" line to Drucker, so no Drucker misattribution is asserted on this page.
